blocks.content: Every distributed system eventually has to answer an uncomfortable question: is that other node still alive, or has it gone quiet because it is dead, overloaded, partitioned, or simply slow this second. Getting the answer wrong in either direction has real cost, so most of the engineering effort in this space goes into managing that risk rather than eliminating it.

Failure detection is the umbrella term for the mechanisms a system uses to form an opinion about the health of its components. Heartbeats, the topic you may have already covered, are one specific technique inside this family: a node periodically announces I am alive and the absence of that announcement is treated as a signal. This lesson goes wider. It covers active health checks where a monitor reaches out and asks are you okay, passive monitoring where health is inferred from the traffic that is already flowing, gossip based detection used by peer to peer systems with no central authority, and the fundamental limits that all of these approaches run into.
Failure detection is not about knowing the truth. It is about producing a belief that is accurate enough, quickly enough, for the system to act on.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain why no failure detector can be both perfectly accurate and perfectly fast, describe at least three concrete detection mechanisms and when each one is the right tool, and walk through a worked example of a load balancer keeping a fleet of backend servers healthy. This is also one of the most common follow up threads in system design interviews once a candidate has drawn a load balancer in front of a fleet of servers, so the last sections connect the theory directly to what interviewers probe for.

blocks.title: Relationship to heartbeats
blocks.content: Heartbeats are the simplest possible failure detector: a periodic I am alive signal with a timeout. Everything in this lesson either builds on that idea, such as active health checks, or replaces it with something better suited to a specific environment, such as gossip in large peer to peer clusters. If heartbeats have not clicked yet, that lesson is the right prerequisite.
1. Why Failure Detection Is Hard

The core difficulty is not an engineering shortcoming that a smarter algorithm will eventually fix. It is a property of asynchronous networks. When a message you sent does not get a reply, there are at least four unrelated explanations, and from where you are standing they are indistinguishable.

["The remote process crashed or was killed.","The remote process is alive but stuck, for example in a long garbage collection pause or blocked on a slow disk write.","The remote process replied, but the reply was lost or delayed somewhere in the network.","The network between you and the remote process is partitioned, and both sides are healthy but cannot currently reach each other."]
items: The remote process crashed or was killed.
The remote process is alive but stuck, for example in a long garbage collection pause or blocked on a slow disk write.
The remote process replied, but the reply was lost or delayed somewhere in the network.
The network between you and the remote process is partitioned, and both sides are healthy but cannot currently reach each other.

blocks.content: This is sometimes summarized as the impossibility of building a perfect failure detector in an asynchronous system. You cannot tell a slow node from a dead node using network signals alone, because both look identical from the outside: silence followed by a late or missing response.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286571027-765793100.png
blocks.alt: A request sent with no response before timeout, where the same observed silence could mean the node is dead or simply slow

blocks.content: Academic distributed systems theory formalizes this as part of the FLP result and the broader study of failure detectors by Chandra and Toueg. The practical takeaway for engineers building real systems is simpler: stop trying to build a perfect detector and instead build one that is accurate enough for the decision it feeds. A load balancer deciding whether to send the next request to a server can tolerate an occasional wrong guess. A distributed lock service deciding whether to let a second process grab a lock cannot, so it leans much further toward caution.

blocks.title: Two generals, one intuition
blocks.content: This is closely related to the two generals problem, where two armies cannot reach guaranteed agreement over an unreliable channel. Failure detection sidesteps the problem rather than solving it: instead of certainty, systems settle for a probabilistic, eventually accurate belief and design the blast radius of a wrong belief to be small and recoverable.
2. Timeout Based Detection

Almost every failure detection mechanism, no matter how sophisticated, bottoms out in a timeout somewhere. You wait for a response for some duration, and if it does not arrive you treat the absence as a negative signal. The interesting engineering is entirely in choosing that duration and deciding what to do with a single missed deadline.
2.1 Choosing A Timeout Value

A timeout that is too short mistakes ordinary variance in network latency or a brief garbage collection pause for a real failure. A timeout that is too long lets a genuinely dead node keep receiving traffic, keep holding locks, or keep sitting in a load balancer pool for far longer than users will tolerate.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Short timeout detects real failures quickly, which limits how much traffic hits a dead node.","Short timeout increases false positives during normal jitter, garbage collection pauses, or brief network congestion."],["Short timeout keeps user facing latency bounded when something does go wrong.","Long timeout is calmer under normal variance but leaves dead nodes serving traffic for longer, which increases user facing errors."]]}

Most production systems pick a timeout by measuring the tail latency of the healthy system, for example the 99th or 99.9th percentile response time, and then setting the timeout at some multiple of that, commonly three to five times the p99. That gives enough headroom to avoid flagging normal slow responses while still catching genuine unresponsiveness within a bounded window.
2.2 Requiring Multiple Consecutive Failures

A single missed deadline is weak evidence. Production systems almost never act on it alone. Instead they require a run of consecutive failures, commonly two or three, before changing a node status. This trades a small amount of detection speed for a large reduction in false positives caused by a single dropped packet or a one off pause.

The same idea appears with retries and backoff. Rather than declaring failure the instant a call times out, a caller retries once or twice with a short backoff, and only escalates to failure detection logic if the retries also fail. This filters out transient blips before they ever reach the part of the system that makes pool membership or failover decisions.
3. Active Health Checks

An active health check is a monitor that reaches out on its own initiative and asks a service whether it is okay, rather than waiting passively for the service to announce itself. This is the model used by essentially every production load balancer, from a cloud provider application load balancer to an in cluster Kubernetes readiness probe.
3.1 How Active Checks Work

A health checker, which might live inside the load balancer or as a separate sidecar process, sends a request to a well known endpoint on each backend on a fixed interval, commonly every one to ten seconds. A quick response with a success status keeps the server in the healthy pool. A timeout or an error response counts as one strike toward marking it unhealthy.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286573175-946781312.png
blocks.alt: A health checker actively probes three servers, two respond ok and stay in the healthy pool, one times out and is flagged

blocks.content: Because the checker controls the cadence and the endpoint, active checks are predictable and easy to reason about. They also work even when a server is receiving zero real user traffic, which passive monitoring cannot do, since there is nothing to observe. This makes active checks the right default for services with bursty or low traffic patterns, and for readiness checks that gate whether a freshly deployed instance should receive traffic at all.
3.2 Shallow Versus Deep Health Checks

Not all health check endpoints are equally meaningful. A shallow check confirms that the process is running and can accept a TCP connection, for example a plain HTTP 200 with no logic behind it. A deep check goes further and confirms that the things the service actually depends on are reachable too.

["Shallow check: process is alive and accepting connections, responds with a fixed status code.","Deep check: process can also reach its database, its cache, and any critical downstream dependency it needs to serve a real request.","Deep checks catch a wider class of real failures but risk cascading: if the database is briefly slow, every instance can fail its deep check at once and the whole fleet gets pulled from rotation."]
items: Shallow check: process is alive and accepting connections, responds with a fixed status code.
Deep check: process can also reach its database, its cache, and any critical downstream dependency it needs to serve a real request.
Deep checks catch a wider class of real failures but risk cascading: if the database is briefly slow, every instance can fail its deep check at once and the whole fleet gets pulled from rotation.

blocks.content: A common middle ground is to run a shallow check on a short interval for fast removal from the pool, and a separate deep check on a longer interval, or exposed on a different endpoint, used for alerting rather than automatic pool removal.
3.3 Health Check State Machine

Rather than flipping a server between healthy and unhealthy on a single probe result, most implementations model status as a small state machine with an intermediate suspect state. A healthy node that misses one probe becomes suspect, not immediately unhealthy. It only becomes unhealthy after missing a configured number of probes in a row, and it can recover back to healthy from either suspect or unhealthy once probes start succeeding again.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286575247-139075766.png
blocks.alt: A three state health check state machine moving between healthy, suspect, and unhealthy based on consecutive probe results

blocks.content: This is the same consecutive failure threshold idea from the timeout section, just made explicit as states so that the rest of the system, dashboards, alerting, and the pool management logic, can all reason about the same shared notion of node status.

With an interval of two seconds, a timeout of five hundred milliseconds, and a threshold of three consecutive failures, the worst case detection time is roughly six seconds from the first missed probe. That number is exactly the kind of trade off a system designer tunes deliberately: faster detection means a lower threshold or a shorter interval, at the cost of more sensitivity to transient noise.

blocks.title: Watch for flapping
blocks.content: A server that hovers right at the edge of healthy, failing two probes then passing one, can flap in and out of the pool. Many implementations require more consecutive successes to go from unhealthy back to healthy than failures were needed to go unhealthy in the first place, which damps this oscillation.
4. Passive Monitoring

Passive monitoring flips the active health check model around. Instead of a monitor manufacturing synthetic requests, it observes the real traffic already flowing through the system and infers health from patterns in that traffic: error rates climbing, latency percentiles drifting up, or connection attempts failing outright.

This approach is central to client side load balancing in service meshes and to techniques like the circuit breaker pattern. A client keeps a rolling window of recent call outcomes to each backend it talks to, and if the error rate or timeout rate in that window crosses a threshold, it stops sending new requests to that backend for a cooldown period, independent of whatever a separate active health check might be reporting.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396524480-167458096.png
blocks.alt: Real client traffic to a backend server observed by a passive monitor, which flags the server unhealthy once thresholds are crossed

blocks.content: 4.1 Signals Used In Passive Monitoring

["Error rate: the fraction of real requests returning a server error in a rolling window.","Latency percentiles: p50, p95, and p99 response time drifting upward relative to the recent baseline.","Timeout and connection failure rate: how often real calls fail to even get a response.","Circuit breaker trips: a downstream client has already opened its breaker against this instance."]
items: Error rate: the fraction of real requests returning a server error in a rolling window.
Latency percentiles: p50, p95, and p99 response time drifting upward relative to the recent baseline.
Timeout and connection failure rate: how often real calls fail to even get a response.
Circuit breaker trips: a downstream client has already opened its breaker against this instance.

blocks.content: The advantage of passive monitoring is that it measures exactly the thing users care about, because it is built from the requests users are actually making. An active health check endpoint can return a healthy status while the real code path that serves actual traffic is broken, for example if the health endpoint skips the exact database query that is failing for everyone else. Passive monitoring cannot be fooled that way, because it has no separate code path to skip.

blocks.title: Where active checks miss and passive monitoring catches it
blocks.text: A payments service has a lightweight health endpoint that only checks that the process is up. A misconfigured connection pool means every real payment request fails with a timeout while the health endpoint keeps returning 200. An active health checker keeps the instance in the pool. A passive monitor watching real request outcomes sees the error rate spike past ninety percent within seconds and pulls the instance out of rotation immediately, well before an on call engineer would have noticed the health endpoint was lying.

blocks.content: The trade off is that passive monitoring needs traffic to work. An instance with no recent requests produces no signal, so a freshly started or lightly loaded instance cannot be evaluated this way at all. That is exactly the gap active health checks fill, which is why production systems typically run both at once rather than choosing one.
5. Gossip Based Detection

Active health checks and passive monitoring both assume something central doing the watching: a load balancer, a monitoring service, a client with a circuit breaker. Large peer to peer systems, such as Cassandra style databases or clusters with hundreds or thousands of nodes, often have no natural place to put that central watcher, and a single central checker polling every node would itself become a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

Gossip based failure detection solves this by having nodes monitor a small random subset of their peers directly, and then spread what they learn through the same kind of gossip protocol used to spread other cluster state. If node B cannot reach node A, B does not just mark A as suspect locally, it also mentions this the next time it gossips with node C, and C passes it along too. Suspicion about A propagates through the cluster the same way any other piece of gossip does, without any single node needing to talk to every other node.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396524480-655647752.png
blocks.alt: Node B cannot reach node A and gossips that suspicion onward to node C, then node D, then node E, spreading the failure belief

blocks.content: 5.1 SWIM Style Protocols

A widely used family of gossip failure detectors follows the SWIM design, short for Scalable Weakly consistent Infection style process group Membership. Each node periodically picks one random peer to ping directly. If that peer does not respond, the pinging node asks a handful of other random peers to try pinging it too, called an indirect probe, which filters out the case where the problem is a network issue specific to the direct pinger rather than the target actually being down. Only if both the direct and indirect probes fail does the node get marked suspect and that suspicion starts spreading through gossip.

The result is a detector whose message load per node stays roughly constant even as the cluster grows from dozens to thousands of members, because each node only ever talks to a small constant number of peers per round rather than the whole group. Detection time grows slowly, typically logarithmically, with cluster size, since suspicion needs to hop through several nodes before the whole cluster agrees.

["Advantage: no central bottleneck, and no single point of failure in the detection mechanism itself.","Advantage: message and processing overhead per node stays roughly flat as the cluster grows.","Disadvantage: information takes multiple gossip rounds to fully propagate, so there is a real window where different nodes disagree about who is healthy.","Disadvantage: more moving parts than a simple heartbeat, including indirect probing and suspicion timers, which makes it harder to reason about and debug."]
items: Advantage: no central bottleneck, and no single point of failure in the detection mechanism itself.
Advantage: message and processing overhead per node stays roughly flat as the cluster grows.
Disadvantage: information takes multiple gossip rounds to fully propagate, so there is a real window where different nodes disagree about who is healthy.
Disadvantage: more moving parts than a simple heartbeat, including indirect probing and suspicion timers, which makes it harder to reason about and debug.

blocks.content: 6. Comparing The Three Approaches

These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, and most real systems combine at least two of them. Still, it helps to line them up side by side against the properties a system designer actually cares about.

{"headers":["Mechanism","Detection speed","Overhead","Scales to","Best fit"],"rows":[["Active health checks","Fast and predictable, bounded by interval times threshold","One prober times every backend, grows linearly with fleet size","Hundreds of backends behind one load balancer","Load balancers, readiness gates, any service with a natural central point to check from"],["Passive monitoring","Fast when there is traffic, blind when there is none","Very low, piggybacks on real requests","Any traffic volume, but needs traffic to exist","Client side circuit breakers, catching failures active checks miss"],["Gossip based detection","Slower, grows with cluster diameter, typically logarithmic","Low and flat per node regardless of cluster size","Thousands of peer nodes with no central authority","Peer to peer databases and clusters, membership protocols"]]}

A production architecture commonly layers these: gossip or a lightweight heartbeat keeps cluster membership roughly agreed upon internally, while a load balancer in front of the whole fleet runs its own independent active health checks, and clients on top of that run passive circuit breakers against individual calls. Each layer catches a different class of problem, and none of them is asked to be the single source of truth on its own.
7. False Positives Versus False Negatives

Every failure detector has to pick a point on a spectrum between two kinds of mistakes, and it is worth naming them precisely because the right answer depends entirely on what the detection feeds into.
A false positive marks a healthy node as failed. A false negative fails to notice a node that is actually down.

A false positive pulls a perfectly good server out of rotation, wasting capacity and, if it happens repeatedly, potentially removing enough servers that the remaining fleet gets overloaded. A false negative keeps sending real user traffic to a node that cannot serve it, producing errors and timeouts for whatever fraction of requests land there until the detector catches up.

["Common causes of false positives: a garbage collection pause that briefly stops the process from answering probes, a transient network blip between checker and target, a health checker that is itself overloaded and cannot send probes on schedule, a check endpoint with a stricter dependency than the real workload needs.","Common causes of false negatives: a health check endpoint that is shallower than the real request path, so it keeps passing while the actual feature is broken, a timeout set too generously relative to user expectations, a threshold requiring so many consecutive failures that a flapping node stays in rotation for minutes."]
items: Common causes of false positives: a garbage collection pause that briefly stops the process from answering probes, a transient network blip between checker and target, a health checker that is itself overloaded and cannot send probes on schedule, a check endpoint with a stricter dependency than the real workload needs.

Common causes of false negatives: a health check endpoint that is shallower than the real request path, so it keeps passing while the actual feature is broken, a timeout set too generously relative to user expectations, a threshold requiring so many consecutive failures that a flapping node stays in rotation for minutes.

blocks.content: Systems where a false positive is expensive, for example a database primary election where flipping the primary unnecessarily causes a disruptive failover, lean their thresholds toward tolerating more false negatives instead: longer timeouts, more consecutive failures required, sometimes a human in the loop before anything drastic happens. Systems where a false negative is expensive, for example a payment gateway where every request sent to a broken node is a failed transaction, lean the other way and accept a higher false positive rate in exchange for pulling bad nodes out fast.

blocks.title: There is no threshold that eliminates both
blocks.content: Tightening a detector to catch failures faster mechanically increases false positives, and loosening it to avoid false positives mechanically increases false negatives. This is a real trade off, not a bug to be engineered away, and naming it explicitly is usually what interviewers are listening for.
8. Feeding Detection Into Downstream Action

Detecting a failure is only useful if something concrete happens as a result. The detector itself is just an opinion generator, a small state machine that outputs healthy or unhealthy per node. The interesting system design questions are usually about what consumes that opinion and how it reacts.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286580265-760177734.png
blocks.alt: A detected failure branching into removing the node from the load balancer pool and triggering failover, both routing traffic to healthy nodes

blocks.content: 8.1 Removing A Node From The Pool
blocks.text: 8.1 Removing A Node From The Pool

blocks.content: The most common action is the simplest one: stop routing new requests to the unhealthy node. This is what a load balancer does the moment its active health check crosses the failure threshold, and it is usually the fastest and least risky downstream action available, since it does not require picking a replacement, only excluding a bad option from a set that already has good ones.
8.2 Triggering Failover

When the failing component is not one of many interchangeable replicas but a singleton, such as a database primary or a designated leader in a consensus group, there is no pool to remove it from. Instead the system has to promote a replacement, which is a strictly more dangerous operation than pool removal because it can go wrong in ways that pool removal cannot: two nodes might both believe they are the new primary, known as split brain, if the failure detection and promotion logic are not carefully coordinated with a consensus mechanism.

["Remove from load balancer pool: fast, low risk, appropriate for stateless interchangeable replicas.","Promote a replica to primary: higher risk, needs a consensus protocol or an external coordinator to avoid two primaries at once.","Trigger autoscaling to replace lost capacity: addresses the capacity gap left by the failed node, usually on a slower timescale than pool removal.","Page an on call engineer: appropriate when the failure is ambiguous enough, or consequential enough, that automated action alone is not trusted."]
items: Remove from load balancer pool: fast, low risk, appropriate for stateless interchangeable replicas.
Promote a replica to primary: higher risk, needs a consensus protocol or an external coordinator to avoid two primaries at once.
Trigger autoscaling to replace lost capacity: addresses the capacity gap left by the failed node, usually on a slower timescale than pool removal.
Page an on call engineer: appropriate when the failure is ambiguous enough, or consequential enough, that automated action alone is not trusted.

blocks.content: A useful design habit is to separate the detection layer from the action layer explicitly. The detector should only ever answer the question of health, and a separate policy layer should decide what action a given health transition triggers. This separation makes it much easier to tune detection sensitivity and downstream action independently, rather than having both entangled in one piece of logic that is hard to reason about and hard to test.
9. Worked Example: A Load Balancer Health Checking A Fleet
blocks.text: 9. Worked Example: A Load Balancer Health Checking A Fleet

blocks.content: Picture a load balancer in front of a fleet of twenty stateless backend servers serving an API. This is close to the canonical setup interviewers ask about, so it is worth walking through with concrete numbers rather than staying abstract.

The load balancer runs an active health checker against each of the twenty servers on a two second interval, sending a GET request to /health with a five hundred millisecond timeout. Each server marks itself unhealthy in the pool after three consecutive failed probes, and requires two consecutive successes to be added back. In parallel, every real request the load balancer forwards is tagged with its outcome, and a passive monitor tracks a rolling one minute window of error rate per server, flagging anything above a five percent error rate as suspect even if the active checks still say healthy.

blocks.title: Walking through a failure
blocks.text: Server 14 suffers a full disk that blocks its write path. Its health endpoint does not touch disk, so active checks keep passing. Real requests that need to write, however, start timing out. Within about twenty seconds, the passive monitor sees server 14 cross the five percent error threshold and marks it suspect, well before the active checker would have noticed anything, since it never checks the disk at all. The load balancer stops sending new requests to server 14 immediately on that passive signal, while an alert fires so an engineer can investigate and eventually replace the instance. Total user facing impact is a few seconds of elevated errors on the small fraction of requests that happened to land on server 14 during that twenty second window, not a sustained outage.

blocks.content: Now contrast that with a cleaner failure: server 7 is killed outright by the underlying host rebooting. The very next active health check probe times out. After three consecutive misses at a two second interval, roughly six seconds pass before server 7 is pulled from the pool. Because there was no real traffic dependent signal needed here, the active check alone was sufficient and faster than waiting on passive traffic patterns would have been.

This pairing illustrates exactly why the earlier comparison table recommended layering mechanisms rather than picking one. The clean crash was caught fastest by the active checker. The subtle partial failure, where the process was alive but a specific dependency was broken, was only caught by passive monitoring watching real traffic. Neither mechanism alone would have handled both cases well.
10. The Interview Angle

Failure detection is a natural follow up once a candidate has drawn a load balancer sitting in front of a fleet of servers, which happens in a large fraction of system design interviews. Interviewers use it to check whether a candidate understands that a load balancer is not magic, it needs to know which backends are alive, and that knowing is itself a nontrivial problem.

["Can you explain concretely how the load balancer knows a backend is unhealthy, rather than waving your hand at it.","Do you reach for a single number, like a fixed timeout, or do you reason about consecutive failures and a state machine that resists flapping.","Do you recognize that a health check endpoint can lie if it does not exercise the real dependency chain, and can you propose a deeper check or a passive signal as a complement.","Can you name the false positive versus false negative trade off explicitly, and tie your threshold choices to which mistake is more expensive for this particular system.","For systems with a single writable primary rather than interchangeable replicas, do you recognize that failover is a fundamentally riskier action than simple pool removal, and mention split brain as a concrete risk."]
items: Can you explain concretely how the load balancer knows a backend is unhealthy, rather than waving your hand at it.
Do you reach for a single number, like a fixed timeout, or do you reason about consecutive failures and a state machine that resists flapping.
Do you recognize that a health check endpoint can lie if it does not exercise the real dependency chain, and can you propose a deeper check or a passive signal as a complement.
Can you name the false positive versus false negative trade off explicitly, and tie your threshold choices to which mistake is more expensive for this particular system.

For systems with a single writable primary rather than interchangeable replicas, do you recognize that failover is a fundamentally riskier action than simple pool removal, and mention split brain as a concrete risk.

blocks.content: A strong answer does not need to reproduce SWIM or cite Chandra and Toueg by name. It needs to show the candidate understands there is an inherent trade off between detection speed and false positive rate, that a single missed probe is weak evidence, and that the action taken on a detected failure should match how expensive a wrong call would be. Naming gossip based detection is a good signal of depth when the system under discussion genuinely has no natural central point to check from, such as a large peer to peer data store, but reaching for it in every answer regardless of fit reads as pattern matching rather than understanding.

blocks.title: A good phrase to have ready
blocks.content: Something along the lines of: we cannot perfectly distinguish a slow node from a dead node, so we tune the timeout and consecutive failure threshold based on how expensive a false positive versus a false negative is for this specific system, and we back active checks with passive monitoring of real traffic so a check endpoint that lies about the true dependency chain does not leave us blind.
11. Summary

Failure detection is the general problem of forming a timely, actionable belief about whether a remote component is healthy, using only unreliable signals like missed responses and observed error rates. No mechanism can do this with perfect certainty, because an asynchronous network cannot reliably distinguish a node that is dead from one that is simply slow.

["Timeout based detection is the foundation everything else sits on, and the real engineering is in choosing the timeout and requiring consecutive failures rather than acting on one.","Active health checks have a monitor reach out on a schedule, which works even with no real traffic but can be fooled by a shallow check endpoint.","Passive monitoring infers health from real traffic patterns like error rate and latency, catching failures active checks miss, but needs traffic to exist to say anything at all.","Gossip based detection lets peers monitor each other and spread suspicion without a central bottleneck, trading some detection speed for scalability to very large clusters.","False positives and false negatives are an unavoidable trade off, and the right threshold depends on which mistake is more expensive for the system in question.","Detected failures should feed into a clearly separated action layer, whether that is simple pool removal or the much riskier act of promoting a new primary."]
items: Timeout based detection is the foundation everything else sits on, and the real engineering is in choosing the timeout and requiring consecutive failures rather than acting on one.
Active health checks have a monitor reach out on a schedule, which works even with no real traffic but can be fooled by a shallow check endpoint.
Passive monitoring infers health from real traffic patterns like error rate and latency, catching failures active checks miss, but needs traffic to exist to say anything at all.
Gossip based detection lets peers monitor each other and spread suspicion without a central bottleneck, trading some detection speed for scalability to very large clusters.
False positives and false negatives are an unavoidable trade off, and the right threshold depends on which mistake is more expensive for the system in question.
Detected failures should feed into a clearly separated action layer, whether that is simple pool removal or the much riskier act of promoting a new primary.

blocks.content: Most production systems do not pick one mechanism. They layer active checks, passive monitoring, and sometimes gossip based membership together, each covering a gap the others leave open, and each tuned to the cost of being wrong in its own part of the system.
The goal was never a perfect detector. It was a detector that fails in the direction, and at the speed, the rest of the system can afford.
